papers.what_it_is: A review written by first-year students of the Bristol Quantum Engineering Centre for Doctoral Training that surveys quantum machine learning algorithms and experiments up to 2015, lists challenges (state preparation, readout, QRAM), and adds an appendix proposing a 'weights in states' quantum perceptron trained with the HHL algorithm.

assertions.value: The authors define three learning categories, loosely based on Aimeur, Brassard and Gambs: L0 is classical machine learning on a classical machine, including machine learning on a classical machine with data that came from a quantum system; L1, denoted QML, runs the learning process predominantly with classical computation with only part of the protocol, such as a sub-routine, requiring access to a quantum computer; L2, also considered QML, has no sub-routine that can be performed equally well on a classical computer.
quotes: First, we consider the classical case, which deﬁnes the category L0.
Also included is machine learning performed on a classical machine but with data that has come from a quantum system
The second category, L1, we will denote as QML.
Here, the learning process can predominantly be run with classical computation, with only part of the protocol (e.g. a particular sub-routine) requiring access to a quantum computer.
We will denote the ﬁnal learning category as L2; this is also considered to be QML.
Here, the algorithm contains no sub-routine that can be performed equally well on a classical computer.

assertions.value: The authors define the Hamming quantum kernel as a sum over measured bitstrings b of the probability of obtaining b, weighted by an exponential factor in the Hamming weight h(b) with the hyperparameter λ.
quotes: Specifically, we group measurement outcomes (bitstrings) by their Hamming weight and assign a weight to each group, modulating its influence on the kernel value:
κHQK (xi, xj ) = |⟨b|U †(xi)U (xj )|0⟩⊗n|2e−λh(b) .
Here, h(b) is the Hamming weight of the bitstring b, and λ is a hyperparameter.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the kernel in Section III, Eq. (6).
assertions.reader_inference: The weight is e raised to minus lambda times the Hamming weight, so the all-zero bitstring has weight 1 and every other bitstring is discounted; the sum over b was printed on its own line in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Hamming quantum kernel matrix has all entries equal to 1 when λ is 0 and converges asymptotically to the fidelity quantum kernel as λ goes to infinity.
quotes: The kernel matrix κHQK will have entries all equal to 1 when λ = 0 and asymptotically converges to the fidelitybased quantum kernel KFQK, see Eq. (4), as λ → ∞.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without a derivation in the paper; it follows from Eq. (6).
assertions.reader_inference: Immediate from Eq. (6), so the FQK is the large-λ limit of the HQK; this is why the paper treats the FQK as a special case of HQK in its hyperparameter sweeps.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Hamming weighting ensures the similarity measure between different data points does not decrease to zero as the system size increases.
quotes: This method ensures that, as the system size increases, the similarity metric between different data points will not decrease to zero.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result or an author claim from one study; not proved.
assertions.reader_inference: No theorem or bound accompanies the statement. Entries of Eq. (6) stay near 1 for small λ by construction, which says nothing yet about whether differences between same-class and different-class entries stay resolvable with a finite number of shots; the paper's evidence for that is test accuracy only.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Hamming quantum kernel is a classical post-processing method based on the same measurement outcomes as the fidelity quantum kernel, and that it avoids the exponential concentration problem by using the full measurement statistics rather than a single fidelity value.
quotes: We introduce the Hamming quantum kernel, a classical post-processing method that is based on the same measurement outcomes as the fidelity quantum kernel.
However, it avoids the exponential concentration problem by using the full measurement statistics rather than a single fidelity value.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result or an author claim from one study; not proved.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper never measures kernel-entry variance or concentration directly; avoidance is inferred from test accuracy.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Hamming quantum kernel rests on the heuristic that similar datapoints on average lead to bitstrings of low Hamming weight, and report in the method figure that the Hamming distributions for same-class and different-class pairs stay distinctly shifted at larger qubit numbers.
quotes: Instead, we use the additional heuristic that similar datapoints on average lead to bitstrings of low Hamming weight.

assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result or an author claim from one study; not proved.

quotes: FQK for QSVM suffers from a major downside: kernel entries exponentially concentrate with increasing system size [8], driving the kernel matrix toward the identity and yielding near-random performance.
Under a polynomial shot budget, this can result in a model that is largely insensitive to the input data and exhibits poor generalization performance.
